terms.tooltipText: distribution shiftDistribution shift is the mismatch between a model's training data and its deployment data. Demonstrations come from a few labs' robots, cameras and lighting; deployment spans unseen homes, objects and clutter. A policy can do well on held-out data from its training distribution yet fail in a new kitchen. Open-world evaluations test this gap: pi0.5 was evaluated in three real homes outside its training set. Lin et al. found generalization to new environments and objects scales with data diversity more than raw volume.

vision-language-action modelA vision-language-action model is a vision-language model, pretrained on web-scale image and text data, adapted to output robot actions. RT-2 established it by encoding actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuning on web and robot data, showing that web-learned semantic knowledge transfers into control. OpenVLA and the π series of generalist policies use the same recipe.

teleoperationTeleoperation is direct remote control of a robot by a human operator, used in robot learning mostly to record expert demonstrations. In the cheap, precise ALOHA rig, the operator back-drives a leader arm twinning the follower joint for joint, so recordings are in the robot's own action space. Mobile ALOHA extended this leader-follower scheme to a mobile base for whole-body tasks.

cross-embodimentCross-embodiment learning is learning from, or transferring to, robots with different morphologies: joint counts, action dimensions and sensor suites. The Open X-Embodiment project pooled data from 22 robot embodiments, and its RT-X policies carried skills across platforms. Each body defines actions differently, and the field aligns them with several incompatible conventions.

success rateSuccess rate is the fraction of attempted episodes in which a policy completes the task, the standard headline metric of robot learning evaluation. A reported rate needs its trial count, time limit and scene distribution. Toyota Research Institute's Large Behavior Model study analyzed 1,800 real-world rollouts and warned of a significant risk of statistical noise from insufficient power. Snyder et al.'s STEP sequential test needs up to 32% fewer trials than the Lai and SAVI baselines.

A reported rate needs its trial count, time limit and scene distribution. Toyota Research Institute's Large Behavior Model study analyzed 1,800 real-world rollouts and warned of a significant risk of statistical noise from insufficient power. compounding errorCompounding error is the accumulation of small per-step mistakes in a sequential task. Each error moves the robot slightly off its training data, where the next is likelier, so total deviation outgrows the per-step rate. Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell bounded it for imitation learning at total cost quadratic in episode length. Action chunking reduces it by cutting sequential decisions.

terms.tooltipText: speed and separation monitoringSpeed and separation monitoring is the collaborative mode in which robot and person may move simultaneously while a safety system continuously keeps a protective separation distance between them. A breach triggers a safety-rated stop. Marvel and Norcross restate the distance publicly as four terms: operator travel during reaction and stopping, robot travel before braking, braking distance, and an intrusion margin plus position uncertainty. The braking term is quadratic in robot speed, so the distance grows faster than speed.

power and force limitingPower and force limiting is the collaborative mode that permits robot-person contact and makes it safe by bounding what the contact can do. Thresholds are biomechanical and per body region. The measurement tradition comes from Haddadin, Albu-Schaeffer and Hirzinger's impact experiments on human-robot collision. Later force-threshold studies report limits by body region and contact geometry.

risk assessmentRisk assessment is the documented machinery-safety procedure for finding a machine's hazards and judging their risks. ISO 12100:2010 is its general-principles standard. Its public abstract covers identifying hazards and estimating and evaluating their risks across a machine's life-cycle phases, with guidance on documenting and verifying the conclusions. The output records each hazard found, what was done about it and why the residual risk was judged acceptable, so the safety argument can be audited.

functional safetyFunctional safety is the part of a system’s safety that depends on its control system working correctly, as opposed to inherent design or physical guarding. For machinery, two standards frame it: IEC 61508:2010 is the generic standard for electrical, electronic and programmable electronic safety-related systems. ISO 13849-1:2023 gives a design methodology for safety-related parts of machine control systems, including software, deferring low-demand operation to the IEC 61508 series. Both treat a safety function as specified in advance, then argued to be correctly implemented.

safety integrity levelA safety integrity level is the IEC 61508:2010 confidence rating for a safety function; it belongs to the function, whichever component implements it. A measured failure rate is not enough: the series also demands avoiding systematic faults, the design and specification errors redundant hardware cannot remove. A learned policy cannot be assigned one, because a level needs a verifiable specification of the function and a policy trained from demonstrations has only behaviour.

performance levelA performance level is the ISO 13849-1:2023 counterpart of a safety integrity level, the rating a machinery integrator in Europe most often must meet. It grades a safety-related control function on a discrete scale, and the standard gives the design methodology for justifying a claimed level. Like IEC 61508 levels, it presumes a function specification checkable against an implementation, which a learned policy lacks.

emergency stopAn emergency stop is a machine function, started by a single human action, that halts hazardous motion. ISO 13850:2015 gives its functional requirements and design principles, independent of energy source, and names IEC 60204-1:2016 for the electrical realisation. It complements guarding without replacing it, since a person must notice the hazard in time. Stopping also differs from removing power, hence the electrical standard's stop categories.

control barrier functionA control barrier function is a scalar function of the state that is positive on a set the system should stay inside. Its derivative condition becomes a linear input constraint in an optimisation solved each step, keeping the safe set forward invariant. Ames and colleagues survey the theory and applications. Because the constraint filters any input, a verified wrapper can enclose an arbitrary, unverified controller and owns the guarantee.

safety caseA safety case is a structured, documented argument, with evidence for each step, that a system is acceptably safe for a given application and environment. The tradition exists because testing alone cannot reach the confidence an autonomous system needs. UL 4600 applies the approach to autonomous products. The Goal Structuring Notation community standard supplies its usual graphical notation, decomposing goals into subgoals until each rests on cited evidence.

conformal predictionConformal prediction is a distribution-free procedure that turns any model’s raw score into a prediction set with guaranteed coverage. Calibrate a threshold for a target such as 95 percent on held-out data, and under exchangeability the sets contain the true answer at that rate. Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer developed it; Angelopoulos and Bates's tutorial brought it into machine-learning practice. In robotics, set size is calibrated uncertainty, so a policy can ask for help exactly when its set is ambiguous.

out-of-distribution detectionOut-of-distribution detection is deciding at run time whether a model's input resembles its training data, so a policy can decline instead of extrapolating. In robotics it runs on the live observation stream and gates the policy. Sinha and colleagues use a fast anomaly detector to trigger a reactive fallback plan while slower reasoning runs. Output uncertainty is a different question: a policy can be confidently wrong on unseen inputs.

terms.tooltipText: behavior cloningBehavior cloning is supervised learning of a policy from expert demonstrations, with observations as inputs and the expert's actions as labels. The recipe predates deep learning: ALVINN (1988) used camera and laser-range inputs and trained on simulated road images before NAVLAB tests. Scaled up, it still underlies most learned manipulation policies; its known closed-loop failure mode is covariate shift.

DAggerDAgger (Dataset Aggregation) is an iterative fix for behavior cloning's distribution mismatch: the expert labels states the current policy visits, and the policy retrains on the aggregate. Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell framed it as reducing imitation learning to no-regret online learning. The task-cost guarantee is existential over the learned sequence and assumes learning and expert-mixing conditions. Linear excess-cost scaling needs a horizon-independent recovery-cost factor u, which can be O(T) at worst.

action chunkingAction chunking is predicting a sequence of future actions in one inference instead of a single action per timestep. Introduced with ACT on ALOHA, it divides an episode's sequential decisions by the chunk length, reducing compounding error and giving the policy temporal context to represent pauses. The cost is commitment to a plan between replans.

CVAEA CVAE (conditional variational autoencoder) is a generative model learning a distribution over a latent variable instead of one deterministic output. ACT trains its action-chunking policy as one, so a single policy covers varied demonstrations of a task. In training, an encoder compresses each demonstrated action sequence into a latent style variable. At test time the decoder generates the chunk from camera images and joint positions, with the latent at the prior mean.

compounding errorCompounding error is the accumulation of small per-step mistakes in a sequential task. Each error moves the robot slightly off its training data, where the next is likelier, so total deviation outgrows the per-step rate. Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell bounded it for imitation learning at total cost quadratic in episode length. Action chunking reduces it by cutting sequential decisions.

temporal ensemblingTemporal ensembling is ACT's execution scheme for overlapping action chunks: the policy runs every timestep and averages in-flight predictions for the current step with exponential weights. In the pinned ACT reference implementation, predictions ordered oldest to newest get weight exp(-0.01 * i), so the oldest retained prediction has the largest weight. Handoffs are smoother, at the cost of one inference per step instead of per chunk.

real-time chunkingReal-time chunking is an inference-time scheme keeping chunked policies responsive when inference is slower than control. While the robot finishes the current chunk, the policy conditions the next on the actions that will already have executed when inference returns, holding that prefix fixed. Black, Galliker and Levine introduced it for flow-matching policies; it tracks moving targets under delays that break naive chunking and temporal ensembling.

flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

terms.tooltipText: action chunkingAction chunking is predicting a sequence of future actions in one inference instead of a single action per timestep. Introduced with ACT on ALOHA, it divides an episode's sequential decisions by the chunk length, reducing compounding error and giving the policy temporal context to represent pauses. The cost is commitment to a plan between replans.

terms.tooltipText: behavior cloningBehavior cloning is supervised learning of a policy from expert demonstrations, with observations as inputs and the expert's actions as labels. The recipe predates deep learning: ALVINN (1988) used camera and laser-range inputs and trained on simulated road images before NAVLAB tests. Scaled up, it still underlies most learned manipulation policies; its known closed-loop failure mode is covariate shift.

compounding errorCompounding error is the accumulation of small per-step mistakes in a sequential task. Each error moves the robot slightly off its training data, where the next is likelier, so total deviation outgrows the per-step rate. Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell bounded it for imitation learning at total cost quadratic in episode length. Action chunking reduces it by cutting sequential decisions.

diffusion policyA diffusion policy is a policy generating a whole action sequence by conditional denoising diffusion instead of regressing one action. Introduced by Chi et al. in 2023, it represents multimodal demonstrations without averaging their modes. It executes only the first few steps of each sequence, then observes again and replans.

DAggerDAgger (Dataset Aggregation) is an iterative fix for behavior cloning's distribution mismatch: the expert labels states the current policy visits, and the policy retrains on the aggregate. Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell framed it as reducing imitation learning to no-regret online learning. The task-cost guarantee is existential over the learned sequence and assumes learning and expert-mixing conditions. Linear excess-cost scaling needs a horizon-independent recovery-cost factor u, which can be O(T) at worst.

imitation learningImitation learning is learning a policy from expert demonstrations instead of a reward signal, by supervised fitting of recorded state-action pairs. Pomerleau's ALVINN (1988) trained on simulated road images before steering NAVLAB; the recipe still underlies most learned manipulation. Its structural weakness: training states come from the expert while deployment visits the learner's own, the mismatch DAgger was designed to repair.

terms.tooltipText: flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

predicted horizonThe predicted horizon is the chunk length H: the number of future actions a chunked policy emits in one forward pass, whether or not it executes them all. It is 16 for Diffusion Policy and 50 actions, one second at 50 Hz, for π0. The committed horizon is how many of them run.

committed horizonThe committed horizon is the number of predicted actions a system executes before a fresh inference replaces them. Diffusion Policy predicts 16 steps and commits 8; π0.7 predicts 50 and commits 15 to 25; original π0, executing synchronously, committed the whole chunk. Real-Time Chunking freezes the first d actions of each new chunk to the values in flight, so the committed horizon can be shorter than the predicted one without pauses.

temporal ensemblingTemporal ensembling is ACT's execution scheme for overlapping action chunks: the policy runs every timestep and averages in-flight predictions for the current step with exponential weights. In the pinned ACT reference implementation, predictions ordered oldest to newest get weight exp(-0.01 * i), so the oldest retained prediction has the largest weight. Handoffs are smoother, at the cost of one inference per step instead of per chunk.

terms.tooltipText: cross-embodimentCross-embodiment learning is learning from, or transferring to, robots with different morphologies: joint counts, action dimensions and sensor suites. The Open X-Embodiment project pooled data from 22 robot embodiments, and its RT-X policies carried skills across platforms. Each body defines actions differently, and the field aligns them with several incompatible conventions.

Open X-EmbodimentOpen X-Embodiment is a 2023 collaboration of 34 labs that pooled 60 existing robot datasets into one standardized format: over a million trajectories from 22 embodiments, covering 527 skills. Its RT-X models, trained on the pool, beat policies trained on each robot's data alone and carried skills to embodiments they saw little of.

end effectorAn end effector is the last link of a robot arm plus its gripper, hand or tool, whose pose the arm exists to place. Kinematics is conventionally the map from joint angles to that pose. Many learned manipulation policies act in end-effector deltas, others in joint targets; across 13,000+ real rollouts, joint space favored control stability and task space favored generalization.

vision-language-action modelA vision-language-action model is a vision-language model, pretrained on web-scale image and text data, adapted to output robot actions. RT-2 established it by encoding actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuning on web and robot data, showing that web-learned semantic knowledge transfers into control. OpenVLA and the π series of generalist policies use the same recipe.

retargetingRetargeting is mapping motion recorded on one body, usually a human's, onto a robot with different proportions and joint limits, so human demonstrations become references the robot can track. Raw retargeting ignores the robot's physical constraints and can produce morphologically infeasible references. H2O and ASAP therefore add reinforcement learning that restores balance and contact feasibility on the real body.

proprioceptionProprioception is sensing the body's own state (joint positions and velocities, orientation, contact), as opposed to exteroception of the outside world through cameras or lidar. It is fast, cheap and never occluded. At ETH Zurich, Lee et al.'s ANYmal controller hiked mud, snow, rubble and vegetation on proprioception alone. Miki et al. kept it as the trusted fallback when the terrain map disagrees with the body.

terms.tooltipText: diffusion policyA diffusion policy is a policy generating a whole action sequence by conditional denoising diffusion instead of regressing one action. Introduced by Chi et al. in 2023, it represents multimodal demonstrations without averaging their modes. It executes only the first few steps of each sequence, then observes again and replans.

flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

real-time chunkingReal-time chunking is an inference-time scheme keeping chunked policies responsive when inference is slower than control. While the robot finishes the current chunk, the policy conditions the next on the actions that will already have executed when inference returns, holding that prefix fixed. Black, Galliker and Levine introduced it for flow-matching policies; it tracks moving targets under delays that break naive chunking and temporal ensembling.

terms.tooltipText: vision-language-action modelA vision-language-action model is a vision-language model, pretrained on web-scale image and text data, adapted to output robot actions. RT-2 established it by encoding actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuning on web and robot data, showing that web-learned semantic knowledge transfers into control. OpenVLA and the π series of generalist policies use the same recipe.

terms.tooltipText: degrees of freedomDegrees of freedom are the number of independent coordinates needed to specify a mechanism's configuration; an arm has one per independent joint. A 7-DoF arm has one redundant coordinate beyond the six a rigid end-effector pose needs, so its elbow can reconfigure while the hand stays put. More degrees of freedom buy dexterity and obstacle avoidance at the price of a larger control problem.

vision-language modelA vision-language model is a model pretrained jointly on web-scale image and text data, so visual recognition and language semantics share one set of weights. RT-2 bet this pretraining helps control: co-fine-tuning on robot trajectories plus the original web data transfers semantic knowledge, like recognizing objects and following instructions the robot data never covered. Later vision-language-action models all start from such a backbone.

flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

terms.tooltipText: affordanceAn affordance is an estimate of whether an available skill can succeed now. SayCan combines it with a language model's usefulness score for the skill. Its learned picking value functions require empirical calibration, and its navigation and placement affordances use hand-designed rules. A high score is not confirmation of successful execution.

vision-language modelA vision-language model is a model pretrained jointly on web-scale image and text data, so visual recognition and language semantics share one set of weights. RT-2 bet this pretraining helps control: co-fine-tuning on robot trajectories plus the original web data transfers semantic knowledge, like recognizing objects and following instructions the robot data never covered. Later vision-language-action models all start from such a backbone.

vision-language-action modelA vision-language-action model is a vision-language model, pretrained on web-scale image and text data, adapted to output robot actions. RT-2 established it by encoding actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuning on web and robot data, showing that web-learned semantic knowledge transfers into control. OpenVLA and the π series of generalist policies use the same recipe.

terms.tooltipText: knowledge insulationKnowledge insulation is Physical Intelligence's recipe for protecting a vision-language-action model's pretrained backbone from action learning. The backbone trains on discrete action tokens with its usual autoregressive loss, while a separate flow-matching expert, behind a stop-gradient, produces continuous actions. On the paper's bussing task it reaches a given performance in 7.5 times fewer steps than π0 and follows language better, in and out of distribution.

flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

vision-language modelA vision-language model is a model pretrained jointly on web-scale image and text data, so visual recognition and language semantics share one set of weights. RT-2 bet this pretraining helps control: co-fine-tuning on robot trajectories plus the original web data transfers semantic knowledge, like recognizing objects and following instructions the robot data never covered. Later vision-language-action models all start from such a backbone.

action tokenizationAction tokenization is expressing continuous robot actions as discrete tokens a language model can produce. RT-2 mapped 256 uniform bins per action dimension onto rarely used vocabulary tokens for ordinary next-token training. It is simple and keeps web knowledge, but 256 bins are coarse and autoregressive decoding is slow; later work used continuous experts and parallel decoding.

The Open X-Embodiment project pooled data from 22 robot embodiments, and its RT-X policies carried skills across platforms. Each body defines actions differently, and the field aligns them with several incompatible conventions.

real-time chunkingReal-time chunking is an inference-time scheme keeping chunked policies responsive when inference is slower than control. While the robot finishes the current chunk, the policy conditions the next on the actions that will already have executed when inference returns, holding that prefix fixed. Black, Galliker and Levine introduced it for flow-matching policies; it tracks moving targets under delays that break naive chunking and temporal ensembling.

terms.tooltipText: real-time chunkingReal-time chunking is an inference-time scheme keeping chunked policies responsive when inference is slower than control. While the robot finishes the current chunk, the policy conditions the next on the actions that will already have executed when inference returns, holding that prefix fixed. Black, Galliker and Levine introduced it for flow-matching policies; it tracks moving targets under delays that break naive chunking and temporal ensembling.

action chunkingAction chunking is predicting a sequence of future actions in one inference instead of a single action per timestep. Introduced with ACT on ALOHA, it divides an episode's sequential decisions by the chunk length, reducing compounding error and giving the policy temporal context to represent pauses. The cost is commitment to a plan between replans.

temporal ensemblingTemporal ensembling is ACT's execution scheme for overlapping action chunks: the policy runs every timestep and averages in-flight predictions for the current step with exponential weights. In the pinned ACT reference implementation, predictions ordered oldest to newest get weight exp(-0.01 * i), so the oldest retained prediction has the largest weight. Handoffs are smoother, at the cost of one inference per step instead of per chunk.

terms.tooltipText: imitation learningImitation learning is learning a policy from expert demonstrations instead of a reward signal, by supervised fitting of recorded state-action pairs. Pomerleau's ALVINN (1988) trained on simulated road images before steering NAVLAB; the recipe still underlies most learned manipulation. Its structural weakness: training states come from the expert while deployment visits the learner's own, the mismatch DAgger was designed to repair.

PPOPPO (proximal policy optimization) is the on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm the locomotion literature standardized on. Schulman and colleagues introduced it as a policy gradient method alternating between sampling environment data and optimizing a surrogate objective by stochastic gradient ascent. The surrogate allows several minibatch epochs per batch where standard policy gradient takes one step. It keeps most of trust region policy optimization's reliability without second-order machinery, and suits massively parallel simulation, whose thousands of robots supply its enormous on-policy batches.

flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

behavior cloningBehavior cloning is supervised learning of a policy from expert demonstrations, with observations as inputs and the expert's actions as labels. The recipe predates deep learning: ALVINN (1988) used camera and laser-range inputs and trained on simulated road images before NAVLAB tests. Scaled up, it still underlies most learned manipulation policies; its known closed-loop failure mode is covariate shift.

success rateSuccess rate is the fraction of attempted episodes in which a policy completes the task, the standard headline metric of robot learning evaluation. A reported rate needs its trial count, time limit and scene distribution. Toyota Research Institute's Large Behavior Model study analyzed 1,800 real-world rollouts and warned of a significant risk of statistical noise from insufficient power. Snyder et al.'s STEP sequential test needs up to 32% fewer trials than the Lai and SAVI baselines.

terms.tooltipText: vision-language-action modelA vision-language-action model is a vision-language model, pretrained on web-scale image and text data, adapted to output robot actions. RT-2 established it by encoding actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuning on web and robot data, showing that web-learned semantic knowledge transfers into control. OpenVLA and the π series of generalist policies use the same recipe.

vision-language modelA vision-language model is a model pretrained jointly on web-scale image and text data, so visual recognition and language semantics share one set of weights. RT-2 bet this pretraining helps control: co-fine-tuning on robot trajectories plus the original web data transfers semantic knowledge, like recognizing objects and following instructions the robot data never covered. Later vision-language-action models all start from such a backbone.

Open X-EmbodimentOpen X-Embodiment is a 2023 collaboration of 34 labs that pooled 60 existing robot datasets into one standardized format: over a million trajectories from 22 embodiments, covering 527 skills. Its RT-X models, trained on the pool, beat policies trained on each robot's data alone and carried skills to embodiments they saw little of.

cross-embodimentCross-embodiment learning is learning from, or transferring to, robots with different morphologies: joint counts, action dimensions and sensor suites. The Open X-Embodiment project pooled data from 22 robot embodiments, and its RT-X policies carried skills across platforms. Each body defines actions differently, and the field aligns them with several incompatible conventions.

action chunkingAction chunking is predicting a sequence of future actions in one inference instead of a single action per timestep. Introduced with ACT on ALOHA, it divides an episode's sequential decisions by the chunk length, reducing compounding error and giving the policy temporal context to represent pauses. The cost is commitment to a plan between replans.

terms.tooltipText: whole-body controlWhole-body control is treating all of a robot's actuated degrees of freedom (legs, torso, arms, hands) as one coupled problem instead of an arm controller stacked on a separate locomotion controller. Model-based versions optimize against the full rigid-body dynamics. Zhang et al. ran whole-body MPC in real time on hardware with plain iLQR and MuJoCo, for dynamic quadruped locomotion and full-sized humanoid walking. Learned versions track retargeted human motion, as H2O did for real-time whole-body teleoperation, with reinforcement learning restoring the balance and contact feasibility raw retargeting loses.

retargetingRetargeting is mapping motion recorded on one body, usually a human's, onto a robot with different proportions and joint limits, so human demonstrations become references the robot can track. Raw retargeting ignores the robot's physical constraints and can produce morphologically infeasible references. H2O and ASAP therefore add reinforcement learning that restores balance and contact feasibility on the real body.

teleoperationTeleoperation is direct remote control of a robot by a human operator, used in robot learning mostly to record expert demonstrations. In the cheap, precise ALOHA rig, the operator back-drives a leader arm twinning the follower joint for joint, so recordings are in the robot's own action space. Mobile ALOHA extended this leader-follower scheme to a mobile base for whole-body tasks.

behavior cloningBehavior cloning is supervised learning of a policy from expert demonstrations, with observations as inputs and the expert's actions as labels. The recipe predates deep learning: ALVINN (1988) used camera and laser-range inputs and trained on simulated road images before NAVLAB tests. Scaled up, it still underlies most learned manipulation policies; its known closed-loop failure mode is covariate shift.

proprioceptionProprioception is sensing the body's own state (joint positions and velocities, orientation, contact), as opposed to exteroception of the outside world through cameras or lidar. It is fast, cheap and never occluded. At ETH Zurich, Lee et al.'s ANYmal controller hiked mud, snow, rubble and vegetation on proprioception alone. Miki et al. kept it as the trusted fallback when the terrain map disagrees with the body.

flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

terms.tooltipText: legged locomotionLegged locomotion is moving on legs instead of wheels or tracks, re-establishing balance at every discrete, intermittent foothold with no continuous contact patch. Conventional controllers were elaborate state machines triggering motion primitives and reflexes, growing more complex without nearing animal generality. The ETH Zurich line replaced them with simulation-trained reinforcement learning. Lee et al.'s ANYmal controller generalized zero-shot to alpine terrain on proprioception alone, and Miki et al. extended the recipe to perceptive locomotion in the wild.

proprioceptionProprioception is sensing the body's own state (joint positions and velocities, orientation, contact), as opposed to exteroception of the outside world through cameras or lidar. It is fast, cheap and never occluded. At ETH Zurich, Lee et al.'s ANYmal controller hiked mud, snow, rubble and vegetation on proprioception alone. Miki et al. kept it as the trusted fallback when the terrain map disagrees with the body.

curriculum learningCurriculum learning is training on tasks that start easy and grow harder as the agent improves. Rudin et al. adjusted each robot's terrain level by its progress. Their documented curriculum-trained policy for simulation and deployment used 4,096 robots, 98,304 transitions per batch and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU. Their separate flat-terrain headline is under four minutes on one workstation GPU.

teleoperationTeleoperation is direct remote control of a robot by a human operator, used in robot learning mostly to record expert demonstrations. In the cheap, precise ALOHA rig, the operator back-drives a leader arm twinning the follower joint for joint, so recordings are in the robot's own action space. Mobile ALOHA extended this leader-follower scheme to a mobile base for whole-body tasks.

retargetingRetargeting is mapping motion recorded on one body, usually a human's, onto a robot with different proportions and joint limits, so human demonstrations become references the robot can track. Raw retargeting ignores the robot's physical constraints and can produce morphologically infeasible references. H2O and ASAP therefore add reinforcement learning that restores balance and contact feasibility on the real body.

PPOPPO (proximal policy optimization) is the on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm the locomotion literature standardized on. Schulman and colleagues introduced it as a policy gradient method alternating between sampling environment data and optimizing a surrogate objective by stochastic gradient ascent. The surrogate allows several minibatch epochs per batch where standard policy gradient takes one step. It keeps most of trust region policy optimization's reliability without second-order machinery, and suits massively parallel simulation, whose thousands of robots supply its enormous on-policy batches.

model predictive controlModel predictive control is constant re-planning against an explicit dynamics model: each step it optimizes a short action sequence, executes only the first action and re-solves from the measured state. Per-step feedback corrects model error instead of freezing it into policy weights, so MPC shows less frozen-policy sim-to-real failure; a wrong model still costs closed-loop performance. Long assumed too slow for full robot dynamics, whole-body MPC now runs in real time on quadruped and humanoid hardware with Zhang and colleagues' MuJoCo-based iLQR controller. Posted in 2025, it was revised in 2026 to appear at ICRA 2026.

flow matchingFlow matching is a generative modeling recipe that learns a time-dependent vector field carrying noise to data, by regressing against the conditional flow instead of estimating a score. In pi0, which brought it to robot control, an action expert trained this way denoises continuous action chunks. Integrating the field as an ODE for a handful of steps is fast enough for high-frequency control and keeps diffusion policies' multimodality.

terms.tooltipText: offline reinforcement learningOffline reinforcement learning is learning a policy from a fixed dataset of previously collected transitions, without new environment experience during training. The trained policy can then be deployed. Its central challenge is distributional shift, which is distinct from ordinary supervised generalization: policy improvement can query action values outside the data distribution, and errors can propagate through Bellman backups without environment feedback. Adequate data coverage and finite-data errors still matter.

terms.tooltipText: PPOPPO (proximal policy optimization) is the on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm the locomotion literature standardized on. Schulman and colleagues introduced it as a policy gradient method alternating between sampling environment data and optimizing a surrogate objective by stochastic gradient ascent. The surrogate allows several minibatch epochs per batch where standard policy gradient takes one step. It keeps most of trust region policy optimization's reliability without second-order machinery, and suits massively parallel simulation, whose thousands of robots supply its enormous on-policy batches.

curriculum learningCurriculum learning is training on tasks that start easy and grow harder as the agent improves. Rudin et al. adjusted each robot's terrain level by its progress. Their documented curriculum-trained policy for simulation and deployment used 4,096 robots, 98,304 transitions per batch and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU. Their separate flat-terrain headline is under four minutes on one workstation GPU.

parallel simulationParallel simulation is running thousands of physics simulator instances at once on one GPU, so one workstation gathers reinforcement learning experience at rates that once needed CPU clusters. Isaac Gym made this practical by keeping physics and policy training on the GPU, passing data from physics buffers to PyTorch tensors without the CPU. That gave two to three orders of magnitude more throughput over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU learner. With PPO on one workstation GPU, Rudin et al.'s four thousand ANYmal instances learned flat-terrain walking in under four minutes and uneven terrain in twenty.

domain randomizationDomain randomization is training a policy across a distribution of simulators with randomized visual appearance, dynamics or both, so the real world reads as one more sample. Tobin et al. randomized rendering and transferred an object detector to a real arm. Peng et al. randomized dynamics and transferred a pushing policy with no real-world training. The cost is conservatism: such a policy is optimal for no single instance.

system identificationSystem identification is fitting a simulator's parameters to a real robot's measured dynamics, shrinking the sim-to-real gap by calibration. Hwangbo et al. found actuator error the dominant transfer obstacle on ANYmal and replaced its miscalibrated analytic model with a learned network from joint-command history to realized torque. It attacks the gap's dynamics component directly; domain randomization only averages over it.

terms.tooltipText: PPOPPO (proximal policy optimization) is the on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm the locomotion literature standardized on. Schulman and colleagues introduced it as a policy gradient method alternating between sampling environment data and optimizing a surrogate objective by stochastic gradient ascent. The surrogate allows several minibatch epochs per batch where standard policy gradient takes one step. It keeps most of trust region policy optimization's reliability without second-order machinery, and suits massively parallel simulation, whose thousands of robots supply its enormous on-policy batches.

reward shapingReward shaping is adding rewards to a task's base reward to guide learning, usually densifying a sparse success signal. Ng, Harada, and Russell asked which changes leave a Markov decision process's optimal policy unchanged. They proved a shaping reward equal to a potential-function difference across the two states is sufficient, and effectively necessary. Classic shaping bugs, where the agent harvests the bonus instead of doing the task, come from non-potential-based rewards, which the theorem excludes.

curriculum learningCurriculum learning is training on tasks that start easy and grow harder as the agent improves. Rudin et al. adjusted each robot's terrain level by its progress. Their documented curriculum-trained policy for simulation and deployment used 4,096 robots, 98,304 transitions per batch and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU. Their separate flat-terrain headline is under four minutes on one workstation GPU.

model predictive controlModel predictive control is constant re-planning against an explicit dynamics model: each step it optimizes a short action sequence, executes only the first action and re-solves from the measured state. Per-step feedback corrects model error instead of freezing it into policy weights, so MPC shows less frozen-policy sim-to-real failure; a wrong model still costs closed-loop performance. Long assumed too slow for full robot dynamics, whole-body MPC now runs in real time on quadruped and humanoid hardware with Zhang and colleagues' MuJoCo-based iLQR controller. Posted in 2025, it was revised in 2026 to appear at ICRA 2026.

domain randomizationDomain randomization is training a policy across a distribution of simulators with randomized visual appearance, dynamics or both, so the real world reads as one more sample. Tobin et al. randomized rendering and transferred an object detector to a real arm. Peng et al. randomized dynamics and transferred a pushing policy with no real-world training. The cost is conservatism: such a policy is optimal for no single instance.

terms.tooltipText: on-policyAn on-policy method is a learning method whose updates are valid only for data from the current policy, so each batch of experience is used once and discarded. PPO, the robotics default, alternates between sampling interaction data and optimizing a surrogate objective that allows several minibatch epochs per batch where plain policy gradient takes one step. This is costly when samples are expensive and nearly free when a GPU simulator yields hundreds of millions.

off-policyAn off-policy method is a learning method that can improve one policy from data generated by another, so old experience stays usable. Haarnoja and colleagues' soft actor-critic, the robotics reference point, combines off-policy updates with a maximum-entropy objective against the sample complexity that keeps model-free deep RL off real hardware. They reported substantially better sample efficiency than on-policy methods on the same tasks.

replay bufferA replay buffer is the store of past transitions an off-policy learner samples gradient batches from. Its contents need not come from the current policy or even the learner. RLPD mixes prior offline data with fresh online experience in one buffer, and HIL-SERL seeds one with human demonstrations before autonomous collection.

Q-learningQ-learning is learning a function predicting the return from each state-action pair, instead of a policy directly, then picking the action its own estimate rates highest. Sutton and Barto present it as the archetypal off-policy temporal-difference control method. Its update uses the best next action, whatever the behaviour policy did, so it can learn from experience it did not generate. Many off-policy and offline robotics algorithms build on it, adding safeguards against value estimates running away on unverifiable data.

sample efficiencySample efficiency is how much environment interaction a method needs to reach a set performance, counted apart from wall-clock time and gradient updates. Minitaur walking used 160,000 control steps over about two hours of the whole training process. A constant-rate budget illustration can turn steps into modelled time; that does not establish algorithm eligibility or predict another robot task.

offline reinforcement learningOffline reinforcement learning is learning a policy from a fixed dataset of previously collected transitions, without new environment experience during training. The trained policy can then be deployed. Its central challenge is distributional shift, which is distinct from ordinary supervised generalization: policy improvement can query action values outside the data distribution, and errors can propagate through Bellman backups without environment feedback. Adequate data coverage and finite-data errors still matter.

hindsight experience replayHindsight experience replay (HER) is an off-policy technique that replays stored transitions with alternative goals and recomputed rewards, alongside original-goal replay. It trains goal-conditioned policies and value functions; relabeling is not restricted to failed episodes or final states. Andrychowicz and colleagues tested it with DDPG on a simulated Fetch arm for pushing, sliding and pick-and-place. Their binary-reward description is qualified by a pushing contact-penetration reward penalty and by starting half of pick-and-place training episodes from a grasped state.

reset-free learningReset-free learning is training on real hardware without a human resetting the scene between attempts. Sharma and colleagues separate deployed-policy regret over training from continuing average reward. Their base setting has no episodic resets; a non-ergodic extension adds a bounded, cost-decremented intervention budget. EARL’s experiments instead schedule occasional resets, reporting learning curves and final deployed-policy performance. Gupta and colleagues chain task-specific policies through a designer-provided task graph, so learned re-centering, pickup and flip-up can restore in-hand reorientation conditions after a drop. Their reported D’Hand/Sawyer training, which also covered pipe insertion, still used supplied rewards and task graphs, motion capture for in-hand manipulation and scripted pickup-arm motion.

terms.tooltipText: domain randomizationDomain randomization is training a policy across a distribution of simulators with randomized visual appearance, dynamics or both, so the real world reads as one more sample. Tobin et al. randomized rendering and transferred an object detector to a real arm. Peng et al. randomized dynamics and transferred a pushing policy with no real-world training. The cost is conservatism: such a policy is optimal for no single instance.

teacher-student distillationTeacher-student distillation is training two policies in sequence for partial observability. A teacher sees privileged simulator state such as exact terrain friction or object pose; a student imitates it using only deployment observations. RMA instead trained a base policy with a privileged encoder, then a separate state-action-history module predicting its latent extrinsics for asynchronous online inference. Lee and colleagues distilled a privileged ANYmal teacher into a proprioceptive student that hikes challenging terrain without ever seeing it.

system identificationSystem identification is fitting a simulator's parameters to a real robot's measured dynamics, shrinking the sim-to-real gap by calibration. Hwangbo et al. found actuator error the dominant transfer obstacle on ANYmal and replaced its miscalibrated analytic model with a learned network from joint-command history to realized torque. It attacks the gap's dynamics component directly; domain randomization only averages over it.

curriculum learningCurriculum learning is training on tasks that start easy and grow harder as the agent improves. Rudin et al. adjusted each robot's terrain level by its progress. Their documented curriculum-trained policy for simulation and deployment used 4,096 robots, 98,304 transitions per batch and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU. Their separate flat-terrain headline is under four minutes on one workstation GPU.

proprioceptionProprioception is sensing the body's own state (joint positions and velocities, orientation, contact), as opposed to exteroception of the outside world through cameras or lidar. It is fast, cheap and never occluded. At ETH Zurich, Lee et al.'s ANYmal controller hiked mud, snow, rubble and vegetation on proprioception alone. Miki et al. kept it as the trusted fallback when the terrain map disagrees with the body.

retargetingRetargeting is mapping motion recorded on one body, usually a human's, onto a robot with different proportions and joint limits, so human demonstrations become references the robot can track. Raw retargeting ignores the robot's physical constraints and can produce morphologically infeasible references. H2O and ASAP therefore add reinforcement learning that restores balance and contact feasibility on the real body.

end effectorAn end effector is the last link of a robot arm plus its gripper, hand or tool, whose pose the arm exists to place. Kinematics is conventionally the map from joint angles to that pose. Many learned manipulation policies act in end-effector deltas, others in joint targets; across 13,000+ real rollouts, joint space favored control stability and task space favored generalization.

PPOPPO (proximal policy optimization) is the on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm the locomotion literature standardized on. Schulman and colleagues introduced it as a policy gradient method alternating between sampling environment data and optimizing a surrogate objective by stochastic gradient ascent. It keeps most of trust region policy optimization's reliability without second-order machinery, and suits massively parallel simulation, whose thousands of robots supply its enormous on-policy batches.

terms.tooltipText: world modelA world model is a model an agent queries to make decisions: given the current observation or state and a candidate action, it predicts what happens next. Policies can be trained, evaluated or planned against it instead of the real world. The 2026 robotics survey requires predictions that change under the agent's action in ways useful for decisions; plausible future images are not enough. The name covers at least six architecturally distinct paradigms, from compact latent dynamics models to action-conditioned video generators.

terms.tooltipText: world modelA world model is a model an agent queries to make decisions: given the current observation or state and a candidate action, it predicts what happens next. Policies can be trained, evaluated or planned against it instead of the real world. The 2026 robotics survey requires predictions that change under the agent's action in ways useful for decisions; plausible future images are not enough. The name covers at least six architecturally distinct paradigms, from compact latent dynamics models to action-conditioned video generators.

terms.tooltipText: vision-language modelA vision-language model is a model pretrained jointly on web-scale image and text data, so visual recognition and language semantics share one set of weights. RT-2 bet this pretraining helps control: co-fine-tuning on robot trajectories plus the original web data transfers semantic knowledge, like recognizing objects and following instructions the robot data never covered. Later vision-language-action models all start from such a backbone.

world modelA world model is a model an agent queries to make decisions: given the current observation or state and a candidate action, it predicts what happens next. Policies can be trained, evaluated or planned against it instead of the real world. The 2026 robotics survey requires predictions that change under the agent's action in ways useful for decisions; plausible future images are not enough. The name covers at least six architecturally distinct paradigms, from compact latent dynamics models to action-conditioned video generators.

latent dynamicsLatent dynamics is a world-model paradigm predicting in a compact learned latent space instead of pixels. The agent learns or plans entirely inside imagined rollouts of a recurrent latent state and reward under candidate actions. Dreamer established training an actor-critic purely on imagined trajectories. TD-MPC2 dropped the image decoder altogether, scoring action sequences under the latent model with a learned terminal value.

vision-language-action modelA vision-language-action model is a vision-language model, pretrained on web-scale image and text data, adapted to output robot actions. RT-2 established it by encoding actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuning on web and robot data, showing that web-learned semantic knowledge transfers into control. OpenVLA and the π series of generalist policies use the same recipe.

terms.tooltipText: world modelA world model is a model an agent queries to make decisions: given the current observation or state and a candidate action, it predicts what happens next. Policies can be trained, evaluated or planned against it instead of the real world. The 2026 robotics survey requires predictions that change under the agent's action in ways useful for decisions; plausible future images are not enough. The name covers at least six architecturally distinct paradigms, from compact latent dynamics models to action-conditioned video generators.

terms.tooltipText: latent dynamicsLatent dynamics is a world-model paradigm predicting in a compact learned latent space instead of pixels. The agent learns or plans entirely inside imagined rollouts of a recurrent latent state and reward under candidate actions. Dreamer established training an actor-critic purely on imagined trajectories. TD-MPC2 dropped the image decoder altogether, scoring action sequences under the latent model with a learned terminal value.

terms.tooltipText: world modelA world model is a model an agent queries to make decisions: given the current observation or state and a candidate action, it predicts what happens next. Policies can be trained, evaluated or planned against it instead of the real world. The 2026 robotics survey requires predictions that change under the agent's action in ways useful for decisions; plausible future images are not enough. The name covers at least six architecturally distinct paradigms, from compact latent dynamics models to action-conditioned video generators.

latent dynamicsLatent dynamics is a world-model paradigm predicting in a compact learned latent space instead of pixels. The agent learns or plans entirely inside imagined rollouts of a recurrent latent state and reward under candidate actions. Dreamer established training an actor-critic purely on imagined trajectories. TD-MPC2 dropped the image decoder altogether, scoring action sequences under the latent model with a learned terminal value.

model predictive controlModel predictive control is constant re-planning against an explicit dynamics model: each step it optimizes a short action sequence, executes only the first action and re-solves from the measured state. Per-step feedback corrects model error instead of freezing it into policy weights, so MPC shows less frozen-policy sim-to-real failure; a wrong model still costs closed-loop performance. Long assumed too slow for full robot dynamics, whole-body MPC now runs in real time on quadruped and humanoid hardware with Zhang and colleagues' MuJoCo-based iLQR controller. Posted in 2025, it was revised in 2026 to appear at ICRA 2026.
